Lebanese Cement Plants Blockaded Amidst Ongoing Border Tensions

A series of blockades imposed by regional actors on key cement production sites in southern Lebanon has disrupted the country’s construction materials sector, with local industry groups warning of deepening shortages and cost spikes.

The blockades, which began late last week and remain in place, have halted operations at Al-Jabal Cement and Phoenicia Aggregates, two of Lebanon’s largest cement producers. According to the Lebanese Construction Materials Union, the affected plants account for over 40% of the nation’s cement output. “We are facing an acute crisis—factories are unable to move materials, and construction projects across the country are already feeling the squeeze,” said Union President Nabil Chahine.

Regional authorities enforcing the blockade have cited heightened security concerns along the border, though Lebanese officials have called the move “an unjustified escalation targeting civilian infrastructure.” The Ministry of Industry issued a statement urging immediate international intervention to restore access to the sites.

Traders report that cement prices have surged by up to 35% in Beirut and Tripoli since the start of the blockade. “We are rationing existing stock and suspending new contracts,” said Rana Hobeika, operations manager at CedarStone Materials, one of the largest distributors in the region. “If this continues, the supply chain will be severely damaged.”

Analysts warn that prolonged disruptions could impact domestic construction schedules and threaten the viability of smaller suppliers. “Lebanon’s construction materials sector is already under pressure from currency volatility and import restrictions. This blockade exacerbates an already fragile situation,” said Fouad Daoud, an independent industry analyst, adding that contingency plans are limited as inventories run low. The situation remains tense as negotiations for access continue.
